{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=agentic+self+correction+epistemological+frameworks+foundational+assumptions&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-94-009-0555-9_19\", \"title\": [\"Some Epistemological Aspects of Present-Day Psychopathology\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-0555-9_19\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1990]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7515259\", \"title\": [\"Verification Independence for Agentic AI: Designing Review Beyond Self-Correction and Multi-Agent Agreement\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><div>\\n As agentic artificial intelligence systems increasingly produce, evaluate, and act on their own outputs, review architectures face a structural problem: adding a second judgment does not necessarily create an independent basis for judgment. This paper proposes verification independence as a task-level design property for agentic AI. Verification independence asks whether the review process is sufficiently separated from the production process to surface errors that the producer is systematically unlikely to detect. The framework distinguishes four dimensions of independence: framing, evidence, mechanism, and authority. It also formalizes a four-function review architecture consisting of a producer, challenger, evidence checker, and acceptance owner.\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n <br>\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n The framework is positioned relative to research on LLM self-correction, chain-of-verification, multi-agent debate, LLM-as-a-judge, correlated model errors, and emerging agentic verification systems. Existing work shows both the value and limits of additional model-based review: structured verification can improve outputs, while multi-agent agreement, self-critique, and LLM judging remain vulnerable to shared assumptions, correlated errors, evaluator bias, and noisy rubric verification. The contribution here is integrative rather than a claim that any individual verification technique is new. It treats independence as a property of the relationship between production and review, not as a synonym for reviewer count or model diversity.\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n <br>\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n The central claim is that a reviewer can provide another judgment without providing another independent basis for judgment. For consequential agentic workflows, reliable verification therefore requires deliberate separation of review roles and, where feasible, external evidence, deterministic tests, independent tools, or distinct authority boundaries. The paper further introduces a qualitative independence checklist, risk-adjusted verification depth, and safeguards against erosion of independence in long-horizon workflows.\\n</div></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7515259\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6566898\", \"title\": [\"Self-Suppressing Correction in Agentic AI Platforms: A Conceptual Framework for Coupled Epistemic Degradation\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Agentic AI systems do not simply answer prompts. They select, sequence, and execute actions across workflows, tools, and institutional settings. This paper argues that the epistemic quality of such systems is shaped not only by model design, but also by platform economics. Pricing, usage limits, feedback pipelines, and adaptive reasoning allocation jointly influence who uses a system, what feedback it receives, how it behaves, and what outputs re-enter public and professional corpora. Existing literatures on platform economics, alignment, and model collapse usually treat one or more of these domains as exogenous. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that endogenizes their interaction. The paper makes three claims. First, sycophancy and user competence interact to contaminate preference signals, especially when platforms rely on author-coupled feedback. Second, fast loops at inference time can drive slower loops in training, institutional verification, and professional competence formation. Third, these coupled dynamics can produce a distinct form of market failure, self-suppressing correction, in which the product degrades users' capacity to detect degradation and thereby weakens the dissatisfaction signal on which market correction depends. The framework helps explain convergence toward stable mediocrity, defined here as an attractor region of acceptable fluency but weakened reasoning depth, attenuated corrective feedback, and degraded verification capacity. The contribution is theoretical and generative: it identifies mechanisms, boundary conditions, and testable propositions for future empirical work.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6566898\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.37514/per-b.2026.3071.2.03\", \"title\": [\"What Do Students Know?
